questions.q: Let ${S}_{a}$ denote the sum of first $n$ terms an arithmetic progression. If ${S}_{20} = 790$ and ${S}_{10} = 145$, then ${S}_{15} -{S}_{5}$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

In an arithmetic progression sum of first $20$ terms is $790$

So, let $a$ be the first term and $d$ be common difference,

So, ${S}_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2} \left[2a + 19d\right] = 790 . . . . . \left($1\right)$

And sum of the first $10$ terms is $145$

So, ${S}_{10} = $\dfrac{10}{2} \left[$2a + 9d\right] = 145 . . . . . \left(2\right)$

By solving equation \left(1\right) & \left(2\right)$ we get,

$a = - 8 & d = 5$

Then, ${S}_{15} - {S}_{5} = $\dfrac{15}{2}\left[$2 \times \left(- 8\right) + 14 \times 5\right] - \dfrac{5}{2}\left[2 \times \left(- 8\right) + 4 \times 5\right]$

$⇒ {S}_{15} - {S}_{5} = 405 - 10 = 395$

questions.q: Suppose ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, \ldots , {a}_{n}, \ldots$~be an arithmetic progression of natural numbers. If the ratio of the sum of the first five terms to the sum of first nine terms of the progression is $5: 17$~and $110 < {a}_{15} < 120$, then the sum of the first ten terms of the progression is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given the ratio of the sum of the first five terms to& the sum of the first nine terms is& $5: 17$,

So,~$\dfrac{S5}{S9} = \dfrac{5}{17} ⇒ \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{2}\left(2a + 4d\right)}{\dfrac{9}{2} \left(2a + 8d\right)} = $\dfrac{5}{17}

$⇒ 17\left(2a + 4d\right) = 9\left(2a + 8d\right)$

$⇒ 34a + 68d = 18a + 72d$

$⇒ d = 4a$

Now~${a}_{15} = a + 14d = 57a$

Also given~$110 < {a}_{15} < 120$

$⇒ 110 < 57a < 120$

$⇒ a = 2 ∴ d = 8$

So,~${S}_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}\left(2 \times 2 + 9 \times 8\right) = 380

$

questions.q: Let the first term a and the common ratio $r$ of a geometric progression be positive integers. If the sum of squares of its first three terms is $33033$, then the sum of these three terms is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given that,

$a^{2} + \left(ar\right)2 + \left($ar^{2}\right)2 = 33033, \left($a, r \in N\right)$

$⇒ $a^{2}\left($1 + r^{2} + r^{4}\right) = {11}^{2} \times273$

On comparing both sides of the equation we get,

$a = 11$~and~$1 + r^{2} + r^{4} = 273$

$⇒ r^{2} + r^{4} = 272$

$⇒ $r^{2}\left($1 + r^{2}\right) = 16 \times17$

$⇒ r = 4$

Now~$a + ar + ar^{2} = 11 + 11 \times4 + 11 \times16$

$= 11 + 44 + 176 = 231$.

Therefore, the required value is~$231

$

questions.q: If $5, 5r, 5r^{2}$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle, then $r$ can not be equal to:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,& $5, 5r, 5r^{2}$~are the length of sides of triangle, then we know that the sum of two sides of a triangle is more than the third side i.e.

$5 + 5r > 5r^{2} . . . \left(1\right)$

$5 + 5r^{2} > 5r . . . \left(2\right)$

$5r + 5r^{2} > 5 . . . \left(3\right)$

From \left(1\right),$

$r^{2} - r - 1 < 0$

\left[r - \left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)\right]\left[r - \left(\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)\right] < 0$

$r \in \left(\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}, \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) . . .\left($4\right)$

from~\left(2\right),$

$r^{2} - r + 1 > 0$~

The discriminant of the quadratic~is~$D = \left(-1\right)2 - 4 \times1 \times1 = - 3$~and we know that if the discriminant of a quadratic is negative and its leading coefficient is positive then the quadratic is positive for all real numbers.~

$⇒ r \in \mathbb{R} . . . \left(5\right)$

from~\left(3\right),$

$r^{2} + r - 1 > 0$

\left($r + $\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)\left($r + $\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$> 0$

So,~$r \in \left(- \infty, - \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$\cup \left(- \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}, \infty\right) . . . \left(6\right)$

Now, taking intersection of~\left(4\right), \left(5\right), \left(6\right),$~we get~$r \in \left(\dfrac{- 1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}, \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) .$

Out of the given options only~$\dfrac{7}{4}$ \text{ and } is not in the interval obtained.

$

questions.q: Let ${S}_{n}$ denote the sum of first $n$-terms of an arithmetic progression. If ${S}_{10} = 530, {S}_{5} = 140,$~then ${S}_{20} - {S}_{6}$ is equal to:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We know that the sum of& $n$~terms of an arithmetic progression with its first term as~$a$~and common difference~$d$~is~${S}_{n} = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a + \left(n - 1\right)d\right] .$

Given,~${S}_{10} = 530$

$⇒ \dfrac{10}{2} \left[2a + 9d\right] = 530$

$⇒ 2a + 9d = 106 \ldots \left(1\right)$

And~${S}_{5} = 140$

$⇒ $\dfrac{5}{2} \left[2a + 4d\right] = 140$

$⇒ 2a + 4d = 56 \ldots \left(2\right)$

Subtracting the two equation, we get,~$5d = 50$

$⇒ d = 10$

On putting the value of~$d$~in the equation~\left(2\right),$~we get

$2a + 4 \times 10 = 56$

$⇒ 2a = 16$

$⇒ a = 8 .$

Now,~${S}_{20} - {S}_{6} = $\dfrac{20}{2} \left[2a + 19d\right] - \dfrac{6}{2} \left[$2a + 5d\right]$

$= 14a + 175d$

$= ( 14 \times8 ) + ( 175 \times10 )$

$= 1862 .

$

questions.q: Let ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, \ldots$. be a GP of increasing positive numbers. If the product of fourth and sixth terms is $9$ and the sum of fifth and seventh terms is $24$ , then ${a}_{1}{a}_{9} + {a}_{2}{a}_{4}{a}_{9} + {a}_{5} + {a}_{7}$& is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, \ldots$. be a GP of increasing positive numbers,

And the product of fourth and sixth terms is $9$

So,~${a}_{4} \cdot {a}_{6} = 9 ⇒ \left({a}_{5}\right)2 = 9 ⇒ {a}_{5} = 3$

Also given~the sum of fifth and seventh terms is $24$,

So,~${a}_{5} + {a}_{7} = 24$

$⇒ {a}_{5} + {a}_{5}r^{2} = 24$

$⇒ \left(1 + r^{2}\right) = 8 ⇒ r = \sqrt{7}$

Now using~${a}_{5} = 3 ⇒ {a}_{1}r^{4} = 3 ⇒ {a}_{1} = \dfrac{3}{r4} = \dfrac{3}{49}$

Then,~${a}_{1}{a}_{9} + {a}_{2}{a}_{4}{a}_{9} + {a}_{5} + {a}_{7}$

$= \dfrac{3}{49} \times \dfrac{3}{49} \times \left(\sqrt{7}\right)8 + \dfrac{3}{49} \times \sqrt{7} \times \dfrac{3}{49} \times \left(\sqrt{7}\right)3 \times \dfrac{3}{49} \times \left(\sqrt{7}\right)8 + \dfrac{3}{49} \times \left(\sqrt{7}\right)4 + \dfrac{3}{49} \times \left(\sqrt{7}\right)6$

$= 9 + 27 + 3 + 21 = 60$

questions.solution:
Given& ${1}^{st}$~term of the A.P$= 100 = a$

And the last term~$= 199 = L$

Let the three~term~be~$a, a + d, a + 2d$

${a}_{n} = L = a + \left(n - 1\right)d$

${d}_{i} = \dfrac{L - a}{n - 1}$

$n \to$~number of terms

Now checking for what value of~$n$~we have integral common difference,

For,~$n = 3, {d}_{1} = \dfrac{199 - 100}{2}$

$= \dfrac{99}{2} \notin I$

For,~$n = 4, {d}_{2} = \dfrac{99}{3} = 33 \in I$

.

.

.

For,~$n = 10, {d}_{3} = \dfrac{99}{9} = 11 \in I$

For,~$n = 12, {d}_{4} = \dfrac{99}{11} = 9 \in I$

So, sum of all common difference that are integer will be~$∑ {d}_{i} = 33 + 11 + 9 = 53$
